# The Vanishing Night

There is a particular kind of darkness that most people alive today have never experienced. I mean true darkness — the kind that falls in the middle of the ocean, or high in a desert far from any city, the kind that made our ancestors pull their cloaks tighter and look up. In that darkness, the Milky Way is not a faint smudge or a photograph from a telescope. It is an overwhelming presence, a river of light so bright it casts a shadow, so detailed that the dark rifts within it — dust lanes where new stars are being born — are visible to the naked eye. The sky in that moment does not look like a dome. It looks like a depth. You feel, viscerally, that you are standing on a planet, on the sunlit side of a rock hurtling through a galaxy.

Most of us have never stood in that light. And increasingly, that absence is not an accident of geography. It is a condition of modern life. The night, as our species knew it for two hundred thousand years, has been quietly abolished, and hardly anyone has marked the funeral.

In January 1994, an earthquake struck Northridge, in the Los Angeles area. It killed dozens of people, collapsed freeways, and knocked out power across the sprawling metropolitan region. In the disoriented hours that followed, emergency call centers in Los Angeles began receiving a strange category of reports. People were calling to ask about a strange, giant, silvery cloud in the sky. They were alarmed. Some thought it had something to do with the earthquake, some kind of atmospheric disturbance, perhaps even something extraterrestrial. What they were seeing, of course, was the Milky Way — the galaxy we live inside, the collective light of hundreds of billions of stars, the sight that every human being who ever lived before the twentieth century knew as well as their own hands. The city's lights had gone out, and an entire metropolitan population looked up and did not recognize their own galaxy.

I think about those phone calls often. There is something almost unbearably poignant about them. It is as if a whole people had been living in a house with a painted ceiling, and one night the paint peeled away and revealed a window onto the universe, and their first instinct was to call the authorities and report the window as a malfunction.

---

For nearly the entire history of our species, the night sky was the most important thing in the world. It was the calendar, the compass, the clock, the newspaper of omens, the great storybook. The Pleiades rising before dawn told agricultural societies when to plant. The pole star told travelers which way was north, long before anyone had a magnetized needle floating in a bowl of water. The Moon's phases structured the first calendars; the word "month" is the Moon's name worn down by use. Entire religions organized themselves around the sky. The pyramids of Egypt and Mexico, the stone circles of Britain, the medicine wheels of the American plains — these are, among other things, instruments for watching the heavens, machines for catching the light of particular stars at particular moments.

And the sky was not merely useful. It was the great repository of meaning. Every culture that ever looked up populated the darkness with stories: hunters and bears, sisters and brothers, crabs and scorpions, rivers of stars, the smoking star, the emu in the sky that Aboriginal Australians saw in the dark patches of the Milky Way rather than in its light — a brilliant inversion, reading the shadows instead of the fire. The night sky was the first encyclopedia, the first shared text of the human race. A farmer in Mesopotamia and a sailor in Polynesia and a grandmother in the Andes looked up at the same lights and wove them into different stories, but the act of weaving was the same. Wonder was not a specialty. It was the human default, available free of charge every clear night.

It is easy to romanticize this, and I should be careful not to. The old nights were also cold, dangerous, full of actual predators and imagined ones. Artificial light is, among other things, one of the great liberations of human history. Streetlights made cities safer. Electric lighting extended the working day and the reading hour; it made night schools and night shifts and night baseball possible. The ability to flood a hospital operating room or a runway or a dark stairwell with light has saved uncountable lives. I would not trade the incandescent night for the dark one if the trade meant giving that up.

But we did not make a careful trade. We made a careless one. We lit the world without ever asking what we were extinguishing, and only in the last few decades have we begun to tally the loss.

---

Astronomers measure the brightness of the night sky, and therefore the darkness of the night, on a scale that will mean little to most readers, so let me put it in plainer terms. Roughly speaking, more than eighty percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies. In the United States and Europe, the figure is higher still. Something like a third of humanity — and the majority of people in industrialized countries — cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, even on the clearest night. The sky glow over a typical city is hundreds of times brighter than the natural background of the night. In the most extreme cases, like the heart of a great metropolis, the sky never gets darker than a deep twilight. The stars that remain visible are the stubborn ones — Sirius, maybe, or Betelgeuse, or the planets, which shine steadily enough to punch through. The rest of the universe is simply gone, washed out like a face lost in headlights.

And it is getting worse. The best measurements we have, comparing satellite images of Earth at night across the 2010s, suggest that the artificially bright area of the planet's surface, and the brightness of that area, has been growing continuously — a few percent a year, compounding. The loss is not a historical event that happened sometime in the twentieth century and is now complete. It is ongoing. People born in the 1990s have already lived under a materially different sky than people born in the 1960s, and children born now will live under a different one still. There is a phenomenon scientists have dryly named "shifting baseline syndrome," usually applied to fisheries: each generation assumes the depleted world it inherits is the natural one. Apply it to the night. Most people under thirty have no idea what they are missing, because they have never missed it. You cannot mourn a Milky Way you have never seen.

The curious thing is how recently this happened. In 1800, nearly everyone on Earth could walk outside and see the galaxy. In 1900, most could. The abolition of the night is largely a story of the last seventy or eighty years — the era of cheap electricity, sodium vapor lamps, and the explosive growth of cities into sprawling, luminous smudges visible from orbit. Astronauts describe the sight of a major city from space as one of the strange beauties of the job: the glowing arterial networks of highways, the bright knots of downtowns, the darkness of parks and seas. It is genuinely beautiful. It is also, from the ground, a kind of theft.

---

The theft is not only aesthetic. Light, like noise or chemical runoff, is a form of pollution, and it has consequences that ripple through the living world in ways we are only beginning to map.

Consider the sea turtle. On beaches from Florida to Australia, hatchling turtles emerge from their sandy nests at night and make a desperate run for the ocean. Their instincts tell them to head toward the brighter horizon, toward the reflection of moonlight and starlight on the water. This works beautifully on a dark beach. On a beach backed by a strip of hotels and streetlights, it is a death trap. The hatchlings scramble inland, toward the glow of the town, and there they die — of exhaustion, of dehydration, of cars, of crabs and gulls that no longer need to work for their meals. Conservationists now patrol such beaches at night, and some coastal towns have passed ordinances requiring amber lighting, or no lighting at all, during hatching season. Whole species are being asked to rewrite their most ancient instincts because we like our boardwalks bright.

Or consider the birds. Every year, billions of birds migrate at night, navigating by the stars and by the Earth's magnetic field, which they somehow perceive — the exact mechanism is still debated — with the help of light-sensitive proteins in their eyes. City lights disorient them. On foggy nights, whole flocks circle illuminated buildings until they drop from exhaustion or collide with glass. The collision deaths get the headlines, and they are grim enough: estimates run to the hundreds of millions of birds a year in the United States alone. But the subtler damage is the disruption of navigation itself, the scrambling of an ancient system of signs. In response, cities have begun to adopt "Lights Out" programs during peak migration, asking building managers to extinguish or dim their decorative lighting from midnight to dawn. In some cities that have done so, bird deaths around prominent buildings have fallen dramatically. The birds, it turns out, do not need us to be visible to them at 2 a.m. Only our vanity does.

Insects, meanwhile, are simply attracted to lights, with a compulsion that seems almost philosophical in its futility. Anyone who has sat under a porch light in summer knows the scene: the moths circling, battering themselves against the bulb, hour after hour. What looks like stupidity is a tragedy of misplaced instinct. Nocturnal insects navigate by the Moon and stars, holding those distant lights at a constant angle to fly in a straight line. An artificial light is close enough that holding it at a constant angle produces a spiral — a doomed orbit around our porch lights and streetlamps. Insect populations are collapsing worldwide for many reasons — habitat loss, pesticides, climate change — and light pollution is one of the compounding stresses. There is a melancholy image in the scientific literature suggesting that the decline of moths, those night-shift pollinators, could echo through entire ecosystems that depend on them.

And then there is us. The human body evolved under a regime of bright days and genuinely dark nights, and it still keeps that appointment. Light at night suppresses melatonin, the hormone that does far more than make us sleepy — it is involved in immune function, in the regulation of other hormones, possibly in the body's defenses against certain cancers. Populations living in brightly lit environments show elevated rates of sleep disorders, and the epidemiological evidence linking nighttime light exposure to disrupted circadian rhythms has grown steadily more sobering. We have, in effect, been running a vast uncontrolled experiment on ourselves, extending the day into the night with the casual confidence of a species that assumes it has outgrown biology. The insomnia of the modern world is not only a matter of screens and worry. It is also a matter of sodium lamps glowing through the curtains, of a sky that never quite lets the body believe the day has ended.

---

What I find hardest to calculate is the cultural loss, because it does not show up in any dataset of bird carcasses or turtle nests.

Every human culture has an astronomical heritage. The Dogon of Mali, the navigators of the Pacific, the builders of Newgrange and Chichén Itzá, the shepherds who named the star patterns that we still use, in bastardized Latin and Greek, every night on television weather reports — this inheritance was free, universal, and identical in its source. No matter where your ancestors lived, they looked at the same Moon. The sky is the oldest thing humans have ever shared.

And we are giving it away not through any decision, but through billions of small, local, reasonable-seeming choices: a brighter parking lot, a floodlit monument, a billboard, a sports field blazing at midnight, a highway lined with unshielded lights throwing half their output sideways and up into the sky, where it does no one any good. Light that leaves a fixture and travels upward is not "lighting." It is waste — wasted electricity, wasted money, wasted night. Estimates of the share of outdoor lighting that escapes upward into the sky commonly run to a substantial fraction of the total. We are, in the most literal sense, burning the Milky Way.

The good news, if one can call it that, is that this is the most reversible form of pollution we have. Smog takes years to clear. An aquifer contaminated with industrial solvents may never recover. But light pollution vanishes the moment the light is switched off. This is worth savoring: the night sky over a city could be substantially restored within a single generation, perhaps within a single decade, if we simply learned to put light where we want it and nowhere else. Shielded fixtures that throw their glow downward. Warmer color temperatures, which scatter less and disrupt wildlife less. Timers and dimmers and the radical idea that a parking lot at 3 a.m. does not need to be lit like an operating theater. None of this requires new technology. It requires only the admission that the night has value — that darkness is not the absence of civilization but one of its conditions, the way silence is a condition of music.

There is a movement, growing for decades now, that has taken this admission seriously. The International Dark-Sky Association has certified dark sky places around the world — parks, reserves, whole communities — where ordinances protect the night. Some towns in the American West, in New Zealand, in the Scottish islands, have become destinations precisely because of their darkness, the way other places are destinations for their beaches. People travel great distances, and pay real money, to see the Milky Way. There is something both encouraging and slightly sad in this: we have turned the night into a tourist attraction, a scarce commodity, something you must travel to, like a glacier or a coral reef. The sky that was once the common property of every human being who stepped outside after dark is now something you must seek, plan for, perhaps even book.

I understand the impulse. I have done it myself — driven hours out of a city, parked on some rural road, and waited for the eyes to do their slow work of adaptation, the pupils widening, the chemical dark-adaptation that takes the better part of half an hour and that a single oncoming headlight can undo. And then the stars arrive, not all at once but in waves, faint ones first and then fainter ones, until the sky is not black with a few points of light but densely, shockingly populated. Everyone who has had this experience knows the peculiar emotion it produces, an emotion that people in earlier centuries would have found puzzling to name because they felt it so often. It is a mixture of awe and smallness and something like homesickness. We are, after all, creatures of that light. Every atom of carbon in our bodies was forged in a star. The line is a cliché by now, but clichés are just truths that have been used too often, and it remains true. Looking at the Milky Way is, among other things, looking at the factory of our own substance.

---

I do not know how this ends. The trajectory is not encouraging. The world is urbanizing, electrifying, brightening. Billions of people are gaining access to electric light for the first time, and I would not dream of telling them they should not have it. The problem is not light. The problem is thoughtless light, unshielded light, light that is sold to us as safety and glamour and delivered to us as glare and skyglow.

But I take some strange comfort in the Northridge phone calls. Underneath the comedy of a city reporting its own galaxy as an anomaly, there is this: when the lights went out, people looked up. They noticed. Something in them still expected the sky to be an interesting place, and when it suddenly was, they reached for the phone. The appetite for the night has not been extinguished. It has only been starved. A species that will call emergency services to report the Milky Way is not a species that has stopped caring about the universe. It is a species that has been locked out of the most beautiful building it owns, and that still remembers, dimly, that there was once a window there.

The night is not gone. It is waiting, the way the stars are always there in the daytime, invisible only because of where we are standing. Switch off the lights, and it comes back. That is more than can be said for most of what we have lost. It may even be enough to hope on.
